planting.note: Plant the tuber with its top at or just above the soil surface in well-drained, gritty, humus-rich potting mix in bright indirect light; Brazilian Edelweiss goes dormant and drops its leaves in winter, when watering should be reduced significantly until new growth resumes in spring.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained, gritty, humus-rich potting mix, watering moderately during active growth and allowing the mix to dry between waterings. Brazilian Edelweiss develops a thick, woody, above-ground caudex over time, topped with soft, densely felted, silvery-white leaves that give the whole plant a fuzzy, frosted appearance unlike the smoother foliage of related gloxinias, with clusters of bright orange-red tubular flowers appearing from the growth tips in summer. Like other tuberous Sinningia it goes fully dormant in winter, dropping all its leaves down to the caudex, and watering should be cut back sharply during this rest period to prevent rot, resuming as new growth emerges from the caudex in spring. Its slow-growing, sculptural caudex makes it a long-lived collector's plant that becomes more striking with age.

planting.note: Plant the tuber with its top at or just above the soil surface in well-drained, gritty, humus-rich potting mix in bright indirect light; Silver-Leaved Sinningia goes dormant and drops its leaves in winter, when watering should be reduced significantly until new growth resumes in spring.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in well-drained, gritty, humus-rich potting mix, watering moderately during active growth and allowing the mix to dry between waterings. Silver-Leaved Sinningia forms a compact tuberous plant with soft, felted, silvery-grey leaves and clusters of small, tubular, red to orange-red flowers in summer, sharing the fuzzy foliage texture of its better-known relative Brazilian Edelweiss but on a smaller, more compact overall scale. Like other tuberous Sinningia it goes fully dormant in winter, dropping its leaves back to the resting tuber, and watering should be cut back sharply during this rest period to prevent rot, resuming as new growth emerges in spring. Its smaller size makes it well suited to a windowsill collection of gesneriads alongside African violets and other Sinningia species.
